title: Ex 8.15 · Removing a set from an intersection
prompt: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be any sets. Prove that $(A \cap B) - C = (A - C) \cap (B - C)$.
answer_format: A chain of lines, each a set (like A ∪ (B ∩ C)) or a statement about an element x (like x ∈ A or x ∈ B). Each line must have exactly the same elements as the line before; start from the left side and end at the right side.
hints: x ∈ (A ∩ B) − C means x ∈ A and x ∈ B and x ∉ C.
x ∉ C is the same as (x ∉ C and x ∉ C), so you may use it twice.
Regroup as (x ∈ A and x ∉ C) and (x ∈ B and x ∉ C), then read each bracket as a set difference.
solution: Let $x$ be any element. Then $x \in (A \cap B) - C$ means $x \in A \land x \in B \land x \notin C$.

Since $x 
otin C$ is equivalent to $x 
otin C \land x 
otin C$, we can regroup this as $(x \in A \land x 
otin C) \land (x \in B \land x 
otin C)$.
That says $x \in A - C$ and $x \in B - C$, so $x \in (A - C) \cap (B - C)$.
Every step was an equivalence, so $(A \cap B) - C = (A - C) \cap (B - C)$. $\blacksquare$

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses Section 8.3 (proving A = B), the definitions of union, intersection and difference (Section 1.5) and the logic laws of Section 2.6.

steps.content: x ∈ A and x ∈ B and x ∉ C
(x ∈ A and x ∉ C) and (x ∈ B and x ∉ C)
x ∈ A − C and x ∈ B − C
x ∈ A and x ∈ B and x ∉ C
(x ∈ A and x ∉ C) and (x ∈ B and x ∉ C)
